overview.central_idea: This page finishes O, covers P (padding, positional encoding, predict(), pretrained models, program synthesis, prompts, PyTorch) and Q (quantization), and covers most of R (RAG, recurrent dropout and layers, regression, regularization, relu, residual connections).

summary:
Index page printed 617 (PDF 641). Locators are **printed** pages: **add 24** for the PDF page.

**O (end).** *overfitting*: recurrent dropout to fight it 373–375 (PDF 397–399). *Oxford Flowers dataset* 520.

**P.** *padding* 238, 239, 322 (PDF 262). *panoptic segmentation* 310. *parameters, defined* 539. *pattern recognition* and *perception* 586. *plot_model()* 199. *PositionalEmbedding layer* 452, 474. *positional encoding* 603. *position embedding* 451 (PDF 475). *predict()* 191, 301, 479, 489 and 115–260. **pretrained models** 256–266 (PDF 280–290): feature extraction 256–264, fine-tuning 264–266 (PDF 288–290). *pretraining* 413, word embeddings 414. *program-centric analogies* 585, 586. *program synthesis* 591 (PDF 615). *progressive disclosure of complexity* 191 (PDF 215). *prompt* 11, 426. *prompt engineering* 568. *PyTorch* 60 (PDF 84): customizing fit() 224, gradient ascent 295, training step functions 217, train_step() metrics 227.

**Q.** *quantization, faster inference with* 561 (PDF 585). *quantize() API* 188.

**R.** *RAG* 501 (PDF 525). *random initialization* 39. *randomized A/B testing* 188. *RandomSearch tuner* 542. *R-CNN* 331. *real-world best practices, lower-precision computation* 556–562. *recombination* 578. *reconstruction loss* 512. *recurrent dropout* 372–375 (PDF 396–399). *recurrent layers in Keras* 368–372 (PDF 392–396). *region proposals* 331. **regression** 104, 126–134, 602 (PDF 150–158), with the California Housing Price dataset and validation using K-fold 129–134. **regularization** 161–168 (PDF 185–192): dropout 167–168, reducing network size 161–164, weight regularization 165–166, loss 512. *reinforcement learning* 214. *relu* 109 (PDF 133). *representational power* 157. *Rescaling layer* 245. **residual connections** 272–276, 370, 603 (PDF 296–300). *REST API* 185. *result()* 208.

concepts.name: pretrained models (index entry)
concepts.definition: Indexed at printed 256–266 (PDF 280–290): feature extraction 256–264 and fine-tuning 264–266.
concepts.intuition: These pages reuse a ConvNet trained on a large dataset to solve a small-data image problem.
concepts.technical: Related entries: convolutional base 257, KerasHub 258, from_preset() 258.
concepts.significance: Reusing pretrained models is how the book handles small datasets in practice.
concepts.misconception: Fine-tuning usually unfreezes only the top layers, after the new head has been trained.

concepts.name: regularization (index entry)
concepts.definition: Indexed at printed 161–168 (PDF 185–192). Sub-entries: reducing network size 161–164, weight regularization 165–166, dropout 167–168.
concepts.intuition: These are the main tools in chapter 5 for fighting overfitting.
concepts.technical: Related entries: L1/L2 regularization 165, recurrent dropout 372–375.
concepts.significance: Regularization is how you trade training fit for better generalization.
concepts.misconception: Regularization does not raise training accuracy. It aims to improve validation performance.

concepts.name: residual connections (index entry)
concepts.intuition: The main explanation is in the ConvNet architecture patterns. Printed 370 applies them to recurrent models.
concepts.significance: Residual connections make very deep networks trainable.
concepts.misconception: A residual connection adds the block's input to its output. It does not concatenate them.
